Monaco editor, SSH/SFTP, Git, and 30+ tools — without the extension sprawl.

VS Code editor core

Every Feature

Six built-in capabilities. Nothing to install.

01

Monaco editor — 100+ languages, persistent settings, format on save.

Tab size, word wrap, font size, line numbers, minimap, bracket pair colorization, whitespace visibility, auto-save interval — all configurable and saved across sessions.

02

Project navigation — file tree, tabs, command palette, Find in Files.

Open a folder to get a full tree. Find in Files searches every file in the workspace, not just open buffers. Command palette (Ctrl+P / Cmd+P) jumps to any file or action instantly.

03

Integrated terminal — multiple shells and sessions, docked below the editor.

Open zsh, bash, PowerShell, Git Bash, or WSL from the terminal dock. Run multiple sessions in tabs. Default shell is auto-detected on first launch.

04

SSH & SFTP — profiles, dual-pane browser, transfer queue, port forwarding.

Group servers by environment. Connect with SSH key or password. Browse local and remote files side-by-side. Upload/download with a queue. Forward ports. Open SSH terminal in a tab.

05

Git integration — stage, commit, and track changes from the sidebar.

Git panel shows staged and unstaged files with M/A badges. Write commit messages and commit without leaving the editor. Branch name shows in the status bar. Modified files are marked in the tree.

06

Built-in skills — 30+ editing tools on first launch, no configuration.

JSON pretty/minify, Base64, URL encode/decode, title case, slugify, reverse lines, sort lines, remove duplicates, trim whitespace, tabs↔spaces, insert datetime, selection statistics, and more.

FAQ

Common questions about features, remote support, plugins, and releases.

Does it replace VS Code or a full IDE?

It covers the most common daily workflows — editing, project search, SSH/SFTP, terminal, Git — without extension overhead or memory sprawl. If you need a full debugger or a large extension ecosystem, VS Code is the better fit. AuroraPad is for developers who want a fast, self-contained editor that handles remote work without switching apps.

What remote protocols does it support?

SSH (key or password auth), SFTP, FTP, FTPS, and SCP. Server profiles are grouped by environment and saved with encrypted credentials via the system keychain. Profiles can be imported and exported.

How do I add my own tools?

Drop a JavaScript file in the plugins folder. It appears in the Plugin menu immediately — no build step, no restart. The plugin API exposes the editor content, selection, cursor position, and current file path.

Which shells does the terminal support?

zsh, bash (macOS/Linux), PowerShell, Git Bash, and WSL (Windows). The default shell is detected automatically on first launch. You can switch per session from the terminal dock.

How does the release pipeline work?

Push a version tag. GitHub Actions builds Windows (NSIS installer + portable EXE), macOS (x64 + arm64 DMG), and Linux (AppImage + tar.gz) in parallel and attaches all artifacts to the GitHub Release automatically.

Are preferences saved between sessions?

Yes. Theme, font size, word wrap, tab size, active panel, shell preference, SSH profiles, and recent files all persist. The editor re-opens to the last workspace and layout on each launch.
